### Invisible tails after oversized inline drawings

ECMA-376 Part 1 §17.3.3.29 defines a soft hyphen as zero-width unless chosen as
a displayed hyphen at a line break. §20.4.2.6–8 describes drawing effect extents,
extents and inline placement. Independent reference controls establish a
compatibility-mode distinction for overflow: mode 14 starts following invisible
soft hyphens and spaces on another line; mode 15 retains them on the oversized
drawing line. Following visible words and manual breaks still advance. The
scanner now follows that modern behavior without changing the older path,
physical drawing dimensions, source offsets or serialized characters.

This is a native reference overflow policy not explicitly resolved by the cited clauses;
it is not asserted to contradict an explicit specification rule. Thirty-two
native control pages and source/PDF hashes are retained in
`tests/fixtures/inline-soft-hyphens`, including effect extents and drawing groups.
All sixteen pages per mode match native text positions within 0.15pt. The former
fitting-picture/discretionary-hyphen gap is corrected: a chosen optional hyphen
retains its identity through layout and does not add a text descender to an
otherwise picture-only line. Its glyph, font minimum, and source caret offsets
are retained. Ordinary text and literal hyphens still form mixed text lines.
Twenty-four additional independent reference controls in
`tests/fixtures/discretionary-hyphen-metrics` cover three font sizes, two picture
heights, and optional/literal hyphen, space and letter tails. All match native
text/wrapping and measured baselines within 0.07pt. The larger-font/short-picture
case also verifies the glyph baseline, preventing a following-line-only offset
fix. Tests retain the 0.15pt two-axis tolerance and editable round-trip checks.
This is native metric compatibility, not an asserted contradiction of the
optional-hyphen visibility rule; all shifted/decorated/bidi combinations are not
independently certified by this matrix.

### Large font sizes up to the 1638 pt editing maximum

ECMA-376 Part 1 §17.3.2.38 (`sz`) and §17.3.2.39 (`szCs`) specify font sizes in
half-point units. The transitional ST_HpsMeasure type also admits positive
universal measures; 1638pt is an editing limit, not an XSD maximum.
Published [font-size documentation](https://support.microsoft.com/en-au/office/fonts/change-the-font-size)
identifies the 1–1638pt range in half-point increments. The shared engine
validator, direct-format mutation, toolbar and style editor now accept that
range, replacing the arbitrary 200pt cap. Inactive `szCs` values are preserved;
this does not remove the active complex-script editing guard.

Nine independently authored native controls in `tests/fixtures/large-fonts`
cover the former boundary, half-point steps, large bold and inherited text,
inactive complex sizing and maximum-size retained text frames. Text origins
match the native reference within 0.15pt and browser tests compare native red ink bounds.
Existing oversized body-line and retained-drawing style-edit guards remain.
No reference/spec contradiction is asserted: this extends the supported subset.

### Paragraph page breaks inside unlinked text frames

ECMA-376 Part 1 §17.3.1.23 (`pageBreakBefore`) generally requires a paragraph to
start on a new page; the clause does not explicitly exempt text boxes. Seven
independent reference controls establish a reference text-frame exception:
first, middle, last and all direct declarations, inherited true and direct false
all retain the same three text lines on the same frame. This behavior is flagged
as a reference-specific exception to the general rule, supported by original XML and
native PDF evidence in `tests/fixtures/textbox-page-break-before`.

Import retains the resolved property and original declarations. Text-frame
measurement suppresses it in a temporary format copy; body pagination and
serialization retain their previous meaning. Paragraphs with omitted format
objects retain default behavior, including in mixed frames containing explicit
break declarations; this is covered by the shape-autofit/script regression. Linked boxes, explicit run-level
page/column breaks and paragraph page breaks inside table cells remain guarded.

If editing geometry cannot be laid out, document opening now retries structured
read-only display before falling back to plain text. Read-only pagination can
retain an oversized line on a fresh page, progressing once per line instead of
creating blank pages until the page limit. Editing remains guarded. An original
two-letter 650pt control has two pages in both the native reference and the read-only
preview; this is not a claim of complete oversized-line conformance.

## First-line indentation after leading pagination breaks

ECMA-376 Part 1 §17.3.1.12 (`ind`) and §17.3.3.1 (`br`) distinguish paragraph
indentation from run-level flow breaks. They do not explicitly define whether a
leading page/column break consumes the first-line indentation. Nine independent
reference controls in `tests/fixtures/leading-break-indent` establish the
compatibility behavior: leading page/column breaks preserve that indentation;
preceding text, spaces, tabs, manual line breaks and list markers consume it.
Both hanging and positive first-line indents are covered. Layout retains source
offsets and break-only pagination lines; serialization and model mutations are
unchanged. Cell-break behavior is separately regression-tested.

Validation: 45 unit tests in four suites, 13 browser workflows, production build,
and 126 XML schema checks across the controls/browser exports and three original
thesis exports pass. Native browser comparisons include wrapping and baseline,
not only page count. No dependencies were added.

### Thesis cross-check of native font weight

The original thesis (#15) independently reproduces the unresolved Demi bold
result: six headings measure 81.95%-82.30% of native ink at 384 dpi. By contrast,
its four isolated Franklin Gothic Book bold words measure 99.99%-100.29%, with
the native PDF explicitly recording the same 9/35pt outline used by the existing
painter. Keep these separate: the Demi face-selection/synthesis gap is real;
the small Book words do not justify any additional emboldening. Source names,
font files and corpus text are not added to production behavior.

## Note marks and automatic line spacing

ECMA-376 Part 1 §§17.11.6/17.11.13 permit ignoring out-of-note reference marks;
the existing importer instead follows the native reference's displayed ordinal behavior.
Section 17.3.1.33 describes spacing but leaves this mark-specific allocation
unspecified. An original 43-case reference matrix now establishes the rule:
note marks contribute their full natural font box but do not enlarge the text
metrics used to expand or compress automatic leading. A note-only paragraph
uses its paragraph mark for those metrics and as a minimum total height,
preserving the note's own descent. Ordinary neighboring text takes precedence
over paragraph-mark formatting for spacing.

Layout carries mark identity separately from stored formatting and separates
mark/literal shaping groups. Measurement retains glyph geometry and natural
allocation, sharing the existing inline-object spacing calculation. No font-name,
source-text or document-specific branch is added. Serialization is unchanged.

The matrix covers literal/footnote/endnote values, Arial/Times New Roman,
baseline/super/subscript, explicit positive/negative positions, single/expanded/
compressed leading, note-only lines, and larger paragraph marks. Native baseline
checks use 0.25pt except the already-existing explicit-position rounding cases
(up to 0.6pt); script ink sizing remains a separate unresolved issue.
Fixture provenance and source/PDF hashes: tests/fixtures/note-mark-metrics.

## Saved building-block content controls

ECMA-376 Part 1 §§17.5.2.11–14 define the document-part gallery, object and
built-in marker. `w:docPartObj` now permits editable saved block/inline content
using the existing persistent-control model. Gallery/category strings and
`docPartUnique` boolean metadata are validated and retained in the original
shell. No gallery chooser or installed building-block resolution is implied;
the specification does not require saved contents to match the gallery.
Existing restrictions on locks, unsupported bindings, nesting and content
remain in effect. No layout, paint or serialization path changes are needed.

Independent native evidence in `tests/fixtures/docpart-object` flags a reference
divergence: its edited Flat OPC XML writes gallery/unique/category,
where CT_SdtDocPart prescribes gallery/category/unique. Import accepts unique
known properties in any order and retains their source order. The native XML
also shows gallery defaulting and removal of inline docPartObj metadata; these
normalizations are recorded, not used to discard source semantics. Native
ContentControls.Count is zero despite four retained XML wrappers, so tests
verify the XML itself. Source and ordinary browser exports pass schema checks;
the non-schema reference ordering is covered separately by a compatibility test.

The original one-page control covers empty metadata, block/inline content,
category/gallery strings and false/zero booleans. Native edits, import guards,
package preservation, edited round-trip, exact undo and browser reopening are
tested. No new dependency, font, third-party engine or corpus-specific branch.

## Large-gap compound borders: layout extent versus painted width

ECMA-376 Part 1 §§17.4.38 (`tblBorders`), 17.4.66 (`tcBorders`), 17.4.80
(`trHeight`) and 17.18.2 (`ST_Border`) identify the relevant declarations.
Independent reference controls show that `thinThickLargeGap` reserves
45 + floor(sz × 2.5) twips per edge, separately from the existing 600-DPI
paint geometry. The 45 twips are the fixed 1.5pt/.75pt bands; the declared gap
drops its fractional twip. This measured allocation behavior is not an
explicit numerical formula in those clauses.

Table writing insets and resolved row-boundary reservations now use that
logical extent. Conflict winners and painted band widths stay unchanged.
Other border styles retain their existing calculation, and paragraph border
layout is unaffected. This eliminates accumulated vertical drift when many
minimum-height rows contain these borders. Source declarations, export and
the authoring UI are unchanged; no extra layout pass is added.

The original fixture `tests/fixtures/compound-row-rounding` covers fifteen
pages, minimum/exact heights, absent-equivalent nil and single-border
controls, and ten sizes including zero and fractional-twip boundaries.
Its 135 row baselines are independently captured from the native reference's PDF and bound
to source/PDF hashes. Browser assertions include all baselines, editable
round-trip, unrelated-part preservation and exact undo. Existing compound
border/frame/corner and row-opposition references cover regressions.

## Nested persistent paragraph-level block controls

ECMA-376 Part 1 §§17.5.2.29 (`sdt`) and 17.5.2.34 (block `sdtContent`)
permit nested block wrappers. The importer now admits nested persistent
paragraph-based controls using the existing ancestor ownership and stack-based
serializer. It retains the depth limit, property validation and unsupported
table guard, including a table under a temporary child of a persistent parent.
Layout and painting are unchanged.

The original seven-case reference control in
`tests/fixtures/nested-persistent-blocks` proves insertion, inner placeholder
restoration, paragraph splitting, replacement/deletion of outer contents, and
mixed temporary/persistent ancestry. The native results retain both wrappers
for edits within a persistent child, remove children when replacing outer
contents, and preserve a temporary parent while editing its persistent child.
These match the existing model's ownership rules; no reference/spec divergence is
claimed. Native Flat OPC and result hashes are retained independently of app
exports. Tests compare native contents and wrapper presence through export,
reopen and undo, and cover search replacement and atomic rejection of a partial
boundary join. Converting such joins to inline controls remains unsupported.

### Native boundary-join matrix (September 25, 2026)

`tests/fixtures/persistent-block-controls/boundary-matrix` records ten additional
reference mutations of the independently authored persistent-block source:
deletion at either outer paragraph boundary, replacement across either boundary,
and replacement containing a paragraph break across the start. Each operation
is applied to both a one-paragraph and a two-paragraph control. Source/result
hashes, selected visible text, complete before/after text, control text and saved
paragraph structure are retained in `reference.json`.

One-paragraph controls become inline wrappers after joins. Text inserted across
the start is outside the surviving wrapper; text inserted across the end belongs
inside it. Two-paragraph controls instead retain their block wrapper and outer
paragraph boundaries. Deleting just an outer boundary has no textual effect;
cross-boundary replacement removes selected letters but retains the boundary.
A paragraph break in replacement text can create another outside paragraph.
Unconditional block-to-inline conversion would therefore corrupt the native
multi-paragraph result. The related OOXML structures are Part 1 §§17.5.2.29 and
17.5.2.34; these structures do not prescribe the interactive deletion algorithm,
so this is a recorded native reference editing behavior, not a claimed schema divergence.

The reference tests verify native-result import, wrapper ownership, text and
byte-for-byte no-edit package preservation. Boundary mutations in the editor
remain guarded. This evidence does not change the template-completion count.

### Persistent rich-text boundary joins: implemented subset

The extended matrix now records 21 mutations plus a converted-placeholder
restoration. The editor implements joins and partial replacements across an
outer edge of paragraph-only rich-text controls. A single surviving paragraph
becomes inline; multi-paragraph controls keep their outer paragraph boundary.
Inserted paragraph breaks across the start stay outside the control. Across the
end they stay inside a multi-paragraph control; only the first inserted line
belongs to a converted single-paragraph control. Aliases, tags and identities
survive serialization; subsequent edits use inline ownership without reopening.
Undo restores source package bytes and the original caret. Attempts to split a
grapheme through conversion reject before committing history.

The native reference rejects partial cross-boundary replacement of a displayed placeholder.
The editor now rejects it too. The additional native restoration proves that
displayed placeholder contents are not a reusable prompt definition: after
entry/clear, the native reference restores five spaces unless a glossary prompt is available.
The inline importer no longer promotes cached display text into that definition.
Declared glossary prompts and their formatting retain the existing behavior.
Relevant clauses also include §§17.5.2.25 (`placeholder`) and 17.5.2.39
(`showingPlcHdr`). No schema divergence is claimed.

Empty inline wrappers, joins spanning deeper internal paragraph boundaries,
nested/scoped bookmark or field ownership, cell wrappers, plain-text wrappers,
and multi-paragraph glossary prompts remain guarded at these boundary edits.
The native empty-wrapper results are retained as the next missing representation;
they are not counted as supported native-result imports or completed templates.

### Empty persistent inline rich-text controls

ECMA-376 Part 1 §§17.5.2.26 (`sdt`, run level), 17.5.2.31 (run-level
`sdtContent`), 17.5.2.25 (`placeholder`) and 17.5.2.39 (`showingPlcHdr`). Empty
persistent rich-text wrappers now have zero-length run metadata. They contribute
no character, width, clipboard text or additional paragraph. Import/export
retains their property shell and identity, including several distinct controls
at one visible text offset. Run slicing, formatting, search replacement and
paragraph joins/splits preserve zero-length owners at surviving boundaries.
Serialization emits the wrapper without synthesizing a text run.

Crossing a block's start and erasing all contents can now produce that empty
inline representation. If a single-paragraph glossary prompt is declared, the native reference
instead restores the prompt inside the converted inline wrapper. Four independent
native cases establish restoration for filled/showing controls, with empty and
nonempty replacement text. The prompt's formatting is retained, and bookmarks
in this newly restored boundary prompt remain guarded pending scoped ownership.
Ordinary inner-control glossary bookmark restoration is unchanged.

`tests/fixtures/empty-inline-controls` includes original XML for start/middle/end,
standalone and adjacent controls, native follow-up operations and glossary
controls. The three prior empty boundary results now import and round-trip
editably. Tests include preserving wrappers during neighbor deletion, subsequent
typing, default prompt restoration, surrounding search/format/split operations,
exact undo and edited reopening. Native PDF and browser pages were inspected;
empty wrappers add no pixels in a same-browser with/without comparison.

Remaining interaction limits: a visible offset does not yet expose the native reference's
separate inside/outside caret positions at an empty wrapper. Typing at the point
uses the existing inside-control default. A native COM paragraph-split request
both returns an error and inserts the default prompt; this API side-effect is
recorded separately, and the editor retains atomic rejection of inline paragraph
splits. Empty temporary/plain-text/picture wrappers remain guarded. These are
interaction limits, not a claimed schema divergence.

## Index entries and fields in rich-text controls

ECMA-376 Part 1 §17.16.5.72 defines XE index entries with no field value;
§17.16.5.29 defines INDEX. Main-story XE entries now retain their instruction,
split instruction runs, delimiter formatting, supported switches (b/f/i/r/t/y),
and zero-width position. Bookmark range arguments participate in bookmark
renaming. Inserting text at an entry leaves it before the inserted text, matching
six independently recorded native reference editing cases. XE is not an empty
editable field result: typing cannot turn it into a visible result, and export
does not invent a separator. Visible XE results remain unsupported.

Cached INDEX results and instructions are retained through editing and export,
including bookmark scopes, using the existing body field model. This does not
generate or refresh an index. Page-story field support is unchanged.

Complex fields wholly contained in an inline rich-text control now retain their
control ownership, including at either boundary. Temporary wrappers unwrap after
content edits and retain the entry; persistent wrappers keep it. Rebuilding a
paragraph writes each field once inside its retained control, and complete
control replacement removes its contained entry. Fields crossing inline-control
boundaries, simple fields and MACROBUTTON prompts inside inline controls, and
controls containing only a zero-width field remain unsupported. Plain-text and
picture control restrictions remain in force. Relevant structural clauses:
§§17.16.2 (fields) and 17.5.2 (structured document tags).

The independent eight-case fixture in tests/fixtures/content-control-index-fields
includes a hash-bound reference PDF, line positions and native editing XML. Unit
coverage additionally exercises ordinary complex field results inside controls,
malformed/crossing envelopes, cached INDEX editing and exact package undo. No
reference/spec divergence is claimed for these semantics. The separately observed
unspecified-default-font baseline difference is recorded with the fixture.

## Standard WMF and native metafile compatibility

WMF recognition now includes the standard 18-byte META_HEADER, in addition to
the existing placeable format. The embedding DrawingML frame supplies a bounded
viewport; the metafile supplies window origin/extents, including negative
extents. This follows [MS-WMF §3.1.3](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/openspecs/windows_protocols/ms-wmf/2678f2fe-df2e-489d-83db-713a9f6397de).
A standard stream must establish window extents before painting. Existing
placeable dimensions, checksums, resource limits and unsupported drawing-record
guards are unchanged. The viewport is session metadata, not rewritten OOXML.

Three native compatibility behaviors are proved independently by the eight-case
`tests/fixtures/wmf-standard` reference:

- The native reference accepts COLORREF high byte 0x02 (PALETTERGB) on the true-color target.
  This differs from [MS-WMF §2.2.2.8](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/openspecs/windows_protocols/ms-wmf/0fdf54fc-6357-4cdd-b27f-795dee14cf86),
  which requires zero. Only ordinary RGB and this flag are admitted; palette
  indexes and custom palette operations remain unsupported.
- The native reference accepts bounded private comments under escape 0x000F. The current
  [§2.3.6.25 description](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/openspecs/windows_protocols/ms-wmf/cfc88064-d86d-4b52-9374-3ce27d456179)
  describes embedded EMF data. The known WMFC signature still rejects before
  editable import; alternate artwork is not silently discarded. Other escape
  operations and malformed lengths remain unsupported.
- The native reference renders WMF bytes under an EMF name/declaration and EMF bytes under a WMF
  name/declaration. The importer decodes the validated payload and preserves the
  original part name, declared type, relationship and media bytes. Missing types
  and vector/raster mismatches remain rejected.

The independent native page provides 15,531 stable interior color samples.
Browser checks exercise original placeable controls and the new standard/header,
comment, flag and naming variants through edit, undo and export/reopen. Unit
coverage includes every truncated prefix, missing/oversized viewport, corrupted
headers, missing window extents and embedded-EMF escapes. Source/export XML
schema checks and native reference reopening supplement the visual checks. These
controls do not establish edge-rasterization equivalence for every cropped WMF;
#23's map edge softness remains an open fidelity issue.

## Percentage paragraph shading and automatic solid fills

ECMA-376 Part 1 §§17.3.1.31 (`shd`), 17.3.5 (`CT_Shd`) and 17.18.78
(`ST_Shd`) define the two color channels and percentage patterns. All 23 named
percentage values now resolve to the flat sRGB colors observed in the native reference, including
the four half-percent names (pct12/37/62/87). The independently captured colored
controls establish rounding of the signed foreground/background delta, with
halfway values toward the foreground. Automatic percentage channels are always
black/white even on dark pages and cells. Both channels still use the existing
validated RGB/theme resolver before blending.

This is native reference rendering behavior, not a document-specific substitution.
The engine's existing resolved-color model and fill renderer remain in use;
original percentage and theme XML is retained on unrelated edits. Only an
explicit fill replacement writes a clear RGB declaration. Paragraph style edits,
source pattern retention, exact undo and export/reopen are covered independently.
Run and cell pattern support is unchanged; hatch patterns remain guarded.

MS-OI29500 §2.1.553 says the native reference ignores paragraph nil shading. The native C36/C37
cases confirm both no-style and inherited-style behavior; nil declarations now
preserve inheritance while their original XML survives exports. Malformed color
channels are still validated.

The same native reference corrects automatic solid paragraph shading: it paints
black regardless of the underlying page/cell fill. The earlier contrasting
black/white paragraph policy was an approximation. Automatic glyph, run shading
and cell shading policies are unchanged. The style editor's paragraph-fill help
now describes black correctly.

`tests/fixtures/paragraph-percentage-shading` contains 60 cases on three pages,
repeated on light and dark page backgrounds, with 120 independent native color
samples and source/PDF hashes. Browser checks sample every native case before
and after typing and after export/reopen. Existing fill authoring, shared-style,
composition, read-only hatch fallback, spacing and seam tests cover regressions.

### Complex field results across sections

ECMA-376 Part 1 §17.16.2 permits any number of result paragraphs between complex
field separators and ends; §17.16.18 defines their matching boundaries.
Sections (§§17.6.18, 17.6.22) do not terminate this field scope. Cached supported
body fields, including nested INDEX/TOC results, now retain their boundaries
across section transitions. INDEX's column switch (§17.16.5.29) is retained;
the stored section properties control cached-result layout. No index or TOC
regeneration is introduced. Table-cell and inline-control scope checks remain,
as does the atomic guard on edits that delete section breaks.

Native reference compatibility: a section-ending paragraph containing only a
field start, field end, empty cached field, or invisible XE entry consumes its
normal line height. A truly empty boundary remains suppressed. A numbered
field-only boundary also displays and advances its list number. This refines
the earlier empty-section shortcut using independently authored native cases;
no source-document identity or instruction-specific layout branch is used.

`tests/fixtures/section-fields` contains three manually authored DOCX controls,
five native PDF pages, 55 measured labeled line origins, and six native edit
observations. Unit/browser checks cover nested boundaries, continuous and
next-page sections, marker-only paragraph height, numbering, reference edit equivalence,
untouched section XML, unrelated parts, export/reopen and exact undo.

### Vector picture effects at display resolution

Supported WMF, EMF and SVG pictures retain their validated vector source when
applying duotone (§20.1.8.23), luminance (§20.1.8.42) or another supported ordered
pixel-effect chain. The unchanged color functions now run at the requested
display resolution before cropping/painting, rather than permanently reducing
the vector to its intrinsic pixel dimensions. Enlargement, source crop, canvas
scale/rotation and tiled fills request an appropriate sample. Raster sources
retain their previous one-time effect transformation. Source media, dimensions,
effect declarations, relationships and serialization are unchanged.

Display samples are reused by resolution and bounded together to four
megapixels, with each dimension capped at 8192 pixels. Eviction closes the
sample; closing the owning decoded image also releases its source and samples.
The bounded LRU retains neither a source vector nor a document. Huge crop/zoom
requests are capped before allocation. Existing raster reduction and sampling
policies remain in force.

The original `wmf-crop-detail` fixture proves the lost-detail issue independently
with standard/placeable WMFs, narrow polygons, positive/negative crops, flips
and chained duotones. Native references bind 968 interior color/gap samples
and sixteen fine-line profiles at device scales 2 and 4. SVG/EMF checks also
cover ordered colors and unchanged enlarged alpha silhouettes. The native
placeable-WMF scale bias under effects remains explicitly recorded in the
fixture README; passing color/detail checks are not full geometric equivalence.
The pre-existing semitransparent luminance rounding gap also remains open.

Existing effect bitmaps are reused when they already cover the requested
resolution. Reductions keep their established transform-then-downsample order,
and a capped display sample cannot replace a larger existing bitmap with fewer
pixels on both axes. Unit regressions cover these preservation cases explicitly.

## Final table row kept with the following body paragraph

ECMA-376 Part 1 section 17.3.1.15 specifies paragraph keepNext chains. The native reference
also carries the first paragraph's keepNext in the first physical
cell of a final table row across the table boundary to the following body
paragraph. It applies even to an empty first cell and when a later paragraph in
that cell has no keep. A flag only in a later paragraph or another cell does not
produce this effect. This is a native extension of the paragraph-only wording.

The five independent controls in tests/fixtures/table-row-keep-next establish
these distinctions. The existing first-cell-keep controls separately establish
that a row does not chain to the next row. Layout now passes the final ungrouped
row's resolved first-cell flag to ordinary paragraph-chain pagination. Source
markup is unchanged. Vertically merged final groups and repeating header groups
remain outside this added behavior pending independent native controls.

## Whole-twip table geometry and percentage preference rounding

ECMA-376 Part 1 sections 17.4.16 (gridCol), 17.4.63 (tblW), 17.4.71 (tcW) and
17.18.87 (ST_TblLayoutType) define preferred widths, twip/percentage units and
layout guidance. The native reference additionally quantizes resolved column allocations
to whole twips before wrapping cell text. It rounds individual widths, then
shares the total-width rounding remainder among leading columns. The 18-page
independent table-twip-widths control distinguishes this from cumulative-boundary
rounding and proves both directions of the resulting word-wrap correction.

For complete rows of positive percentage cell preferences at an explicit table
width, the native reference first normalizes shares in whole 1/50-percent units, then allocates
their twip widths while retaining the row total. A separate 12-page control
establishes this intermediate precision for fixed and AutoFit tables. Applying
only final twip rounding gives incorrect allocations. These numerical rounding
steps are observed reference compatibility behavior, beyond the layout clause's
optional algorithm description.

Resolution uses temporary preference copies; imported grid and percent values
are unchanged by layout/export. Mixed-unit rows, omitted grid columns and tables
without an explicit width keep their existing preference resolution. Degenerate
sub-twip allocations that cannot round to positive columns keep their previous
geometry pending separate native controls. Native PDFs, COM widths and source
hashes are retained in tests/fixtures/table-twip-widths. The browser checks compare
actual cell widths and line breaks independently of the production algorithm.

### Narrow-cell word-fit boundary: pending native discrepancy

The independent `tests/fixtures/native-fit-boundary` control covers 20 fixed and
AutoFit tables, with explicit Arial bold 20pt, kerning and zero cell margins.
All source/reference PDF/case hashes are recorded. The native reference keeps the complete
word at a fixed width of 2875 twips; the browser splits it through 2881 twips.
The native reference expands the three smaller AutoFit preferences to 2875 twips. Browser
measurement is 2881.444 twips, and integer grid rounding leaves some AutoFit
cells fractionally narrower than their measured minimum. All three page pairs
were inspected; import/edit/reopen, exact no-edit/undo and unrelated-part checks
passed. Source plus three browser exports passed transitional XSD validation.

Relevant declarations are Part 1 sections 17.4.52 (`tblLayout`), 17.4.63
(`tblW`), 17.4.71 (`tcW`) and 17.18.87 (`ST_TblLayoutType`). The remaining issue
is native text measurement/line fitting at these boundaries. These observations
do not establish a universal rounding tolerance or prove a specification
violation. No production change or rendering-conformance pass is claimed.
Further words and ending glyphs must separate advance rounding from trailing
bearings before a general correction is selected.

## AutoFit minimum preservation during column rounding

Final whole-twip balancing now retains feasible individual-column content
minimums. Previously, subtracting the total's rounding remainder from a leading
column could undo AutoFit's minimum allocation and split an otherwise fitting
word. A column below its minimum receives space from columns with spare width;
the total remains unchanged. Compressed allocations that cannot satisfy their
word minimums retain the existing wrapping behavior. This does not implement a
complete integer solver for merged-span minimum constraints.

The independently authored `autofit-rounding-minimum` fixture covers twelve
three-, four- and five-column tables at four preferred widths. The native reference
keeps all 48 cell texts on one line; the former engine split two.
The regression verifies native text positions, package preservation, editing,
undo and reopening. ECMA-376 Part 1 §§17.4.52, 17.4.63, 17.4.71 and 17.18.87
provide the layout/preferred-width context. This is a reference-compatible rounding
detail within the specification's algorithm flexibility, not an established
normative contradiction.

## Following-space kerning and whole-twip AutoFit minima

The pending narrow-cell discrepancy above is resolved by preserving shaping
context rather than adding an overflow tolerance. Part 1 section 17.3.2.19
(`kern`) enables font pair adjustments at the stored threshold. The native reference includes
the final glyph's pair with a following ordinary space when fitting the word,
while excluding the hanging space's own advance. The context survives an
identical-format or color-only run split; font/kerning boundaries, tabs,
manual breaks and paragraph ends do not supply that pair. Line fitting,
content alignment, the word-end caret and intrinsic widths now use this
context. The long-space-tail path retains bounded shaping work.

The AutoFit content minimum is rounded upward to a whole twip before grid
allocation, preventing direct nearest-twip truncation of the measured minimum. Authored `tblW`, `tcW`
and grid values remain unchanged. This is native numerical evidence refining
sections 17.4.52, 17.4.63, 17.4.71 and 17.18.87, not an identified reference/spec
violation. No word, font or document name appears in the implementation.

`tests/fixtures/trailing-space-kerning` contains 19 independently authored
controls with native PDF/cell-width evidence across four font families and
regular, bold and italic faces. Together with the prior 20 boundary controls,
39 native line-break/width cases are checked in the browser, including edits,
export, exact undo and reopen. Native fidelity tests explicitly require the
reference fonts; the synthetic line-fit/caret/alignment/boundary tests remain
portable. The focused native fixture still exposes an unrelated row-splitting
pagination difference, documented in its README.


## Absent run-default category and kerning

ECMA-376 Part 1 §17.7.5.5 (`rPrDefault`) explicitly makes run defaults
application-defined when that category is absent. The native reference supplies a
1pt kerning threshold in that case, including absent styles and empty
`docDefaults`. A present empty category instead leaves kerning off; explicit
default, style and direct thresholds continue through the existing cascade
under §17.3.2.19. The importer now preserves that distinction without adding
XML declarations to retained packages. New documents declare `rPrDefault`
and retain their existing unkerned default. No per-line probe or new shaping
pass is introduced by this import-time default selection.

Six original controls in `tests/fixtures/default-kerning` retain 48 native
paragraph thresholds and their PDF geometry. They were found while isolating
the reviewed-family Open Sans discrepancy: that older control omitted
`rPrDefault`, so the native reference enabled kerning while the browser disabled it. Separate
font-version and font-table differences remain unresolved. The default
selection is allowed consumer behavior, not a reference/spec contradiction.

## Selecting installed fonts

The font picker can enumerate local font families after the user selects
“Browse installed fonts” and grants browser access. The list retains names
and browser font handles in session memory. With access already granted,
ambiguous font faces can also have their local metadata read as described
below. Font files are not persisted, uploaded, embedded, or served.
Enumeration follows the browser Local Font Access API and is available only
where that API is exposed (normally desktop Chromium in a secure context).
Other browsers, and users who decline enumeration, can enter an installed
font name. Availability is checked before applying the choice.

Selection uses the existing ECMA-376 Part 1 §17.3.2.26 (`rFonts`) path: only
Latin `ascii`/`hAnsi` declarations change; East Asian and complex-script slots,
untouched package parts, and the existing undo behavior are retained. This
is a picker extension, not a change to font substitution or native reference shaping.
The independent `editor-ux.docx` fixture covers selection, export, undo/redo
and reopening through both entry paths. Browser tests also cover denial,
missing fonts, duplicate faces and closing an outstanding enumeration.

Reference: https://wicg.github.io/local-font-access/

## Synthetic-bold glyph advances

The original `tests/fixtures/synthetic-bold-advance` controls retain 70 native reference
fit thresholds across four controls. They cover ordinary/real-bold/heavy
faces, synthetic bold at different sizes and units-per-em, combining marks,
explicit standard ligatures, and medium/semibold weight boundaries.

For a confirmed synthesized fixed face, a private in-memory FontFace adds one
font design unit to each positive hmtx advance; zero-advance marks and shared
trailing metrics retain their structure. Outlines, GSUB, GPOS and kerning
remain unchanged. hhea.advanceWidthMax and SFNT checksums are rebuilt, with
stale DSIG and hdmx removed. Measurement and painting use this same face;
Canvas letterSpacing is not used to simulate the adjustment. Registered bold
weight prevents browser double synthesis and retains bold fallback selection.
The native stroke decision remains separate from the advance decision.

Local bytes are obtained only through already-authorized Local Font Access;
the existing picker requests that permission. Reviewed same-origin font
assets can also supply bytes. No fonts are written to DOCX, disk or network.
Denied access, font collections, variable fonts and malformed metadata retain
the existing approximation. Real bold and already-heavy faces are excluded.
The original strict synthetic-width oracles now pass, including all 70 native
whole-twip thresholds; the separate Dubai ink oracle now also passes with
authorized metadata, as described below.

ECMA-376 §17.3.2.1 and §17.3.2.26 do not prescribe this synthesis metric;
this is native reference compatibility, not a proven spec divergence. SFNT handling follows
[OpenType hmtx](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/typography/opentype/spec/hmtx)
and [hhea](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/typography/opentype/spec/hhea).

## Authorized local-face metadata and synthetic bold ink

When the existing raster comparison cannot distinguish an ordinary named
face from an already-heavy one, the renderer can read metadata through the
browser Local Font Access API, only if permission is already granted. It
never prompts during document loading. The picker is the explicit access
request. Only full/PostScript-name matches are used; a family-only match is
not sufficient to identify the face. Metadata reads are lazy and coalesced;
source buffers are not persisted; derived advance faces live only in browser
memory and are not written to the document or network.
Granting access through the picker invalidates prior preparation results.

The original SFNT metadata reader bounds-checks table records and reads
`head.unitsPerEm`, `OS/2.usWeightClass` and `OS/2.fsSelection`. A fixed face
with light/normal weight (exactly 300 or 400) and no bold selection bit can take the existing em/35
synthetic stroke when both regular and forced-bold ink match the browser's
unchanged face. Variable fonts retain the prior detection policy. Metadata
failure, denied/unavailable access, and ambiguous names retain the previous
behavior. No font-name special cases or document declarations are introduced.

This resolves the Franklin Gothic Demi and Demi Italic ink ambiguity on
user-authorized devices. The original 24-case `synthetic-bold` control now
has a hash-bound 384dpi ink reference: eight regular/bold/italic samples for
Demi and Arial Black stay within the existing 5% native ink tolerance. Demi
bold and bold-italic differ by approximately 0.2% on the reference machine;
Arial Black receives no extra stroke. Editing, export, exact undo and reopen
are covered. Advance/line-fit correction is covered separately above.

ECMA-376 §17.3.2.1 and §17.3.2.26 describe the bold/font declarations;
OpenType metadata interpretation follows the
[font file structure](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/typography/opentype/spec/otff),
[`head`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/typography/opentype/spec/head) and
[`OS/2`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/typography/opentype/spec/os2)
specifications. The native reference's synthesis choice is compatibility behavior; no new
spec contradiction is claimed.

The independent `synthetic-bold-weight-metadata` follow-up varies only OS/2
weight and unique font names across 21 otherwise identical OFL-derived faces.
The native reference's five-page export contains a stroke only at weights 300 and 400; the
immediate neighbors 299/301 and 399/401 do not receive one. This refines the
earlier at-most-400 assumption. The metadata check now also applies when the
browser already synthesizes bold, removing the excess stroke from Dubai Medium
and Segoe UI Semilight. The existing advance correction remains independent.
Eight native 384dpi regular/bold samples pass the unchanged 5% ink bound, and
all 70 whole-twip advance thresholds still pass. Unknown/denied metadata retain
the previous approximation; no global weight rule is applied without an exact
local-face match and the existing raster checks. Font preparation reads the
cached metadata; no new per-glyph or per-layout work is introduced.

## SVG backdrop compositing: native versus PDF raster evidence

`tests/fixtures/svg-backdrop-compositing` retains 36 original samples with
varied opaque backdrops, solid fills, alpha and overlaps. Native reference PDF output,
the native reference's `Range.EnhMetaFileBits`, the nested SVG metafile and a GDI+ raster are
hash-bound. Exact RGB comparisons use the metafile/GDI+ result; PDFium colors
are retained separately. A cross-check with Poppler showed that the same PDF
can produce different channel bytes, so PDF raster colors alone are not proof
of a reference screen mismatch. No specification contradiction is asserted.

The strict browser oracle remains an explicit expected failure. These controls
have backgrounds inside the SVG; they do not cover a transparent SVG later
composited over a DOCX page/cell background. The internal gray overlap nevertheless reproduces corpus #57's exact RGB
difference. Eight of 36 browser samples differ from GDI+. Separately rounding
source and destination contributions reproduces the 36 native samples, but
a general background/coverage-aware implementation is still outstanding. This change adds evidence, not a production
compositing correction, and does not widen existing rendering tolerances.

the existing per-face cache rather than adding work to character measurement.

## Mixed automatic cell widths and merged constraints

`mixed-cell-width-preferences` began with 16 original native reference controls
with hash-bound cell-fill geometry. The fixed correction below resolved eight
cases; the subsequent AutoFit correction resolves the remaining cases and
adds independent noWrap and four-column coverage.

and merged header/footer constraints. ECMA-376 Part 1 sections 17.4.49,
17.4.63, 17.4.71 and 17.18.87 apply. The permitted algorithm flexibility means
these are reference-compatibility gaps, not established normative contradictions.
Corpus #64 still has a residual width discrepancy; see the AutoFit entry below.


### Fixed merged preference ordering

The fixed-layout subset of `mixed-cell-width-preferences` now matches all eight
native cases. Automatic/omitted merged widths retain the current span, and
explicit merged requests are deferred until individual column preferences
are read. Resolving inner spans before enclosing spans avoids expanding a
full row twice and then proportionally shrinking otherwise valid columns.
The original stored grid and cell declarations remain unchanged.

The existing native fixed preference/reduction suites also pass. The
AutoFit path remained separate at this checkpoint; this
change does not claim to resolve corpus #64's AutoFit width defect. The same
ECMA-376 guidance clauses listed above apply; this refines reference compatibility
without claiming a new normative spec contradiction.

### AutoFit mixed explicit and automatic preferences

Keep explicit single-column requests while distributing surplus among
unspecified columns. A merged preferred width determines one remaining column;
when multiple columns are unspecified, resize the span together. Measure merged
content against the combined known preferences before adding content pressure.
Enforce minima before holding columns fixed and after proportional expansion,
so noWrap does not accidentally cause unrelated preferred columns to grow.
The saved grid, cell widths and package contents remain untouched.

All 38 native control cases now pass the unchanged 0.2pt x/width tolerance:
16 original, 16 noWrap variants and six four-column cases. The browser suite
also checks no-edit package preservation, body editing, exact undo and reopen.
Existing growth (three compatibility cases), cell preferences (two modes),
span pressure, repeated spans, merged-table editing and noWrap remain covered.
One optional private merged-card test is skipped when its source is absent.
25 focused unit tests pass. Both new source fixtures and 55 XML parts from
browser exports pass transitional XSD. Production build/license gate pass.

A protected absolute noWrap width now contributes to the minimum constraint
without being spread across columns as measured content. The measured maximum
can therefore be smaller than the protected minimum; table-level minima still
constrain allocation. Mixed-column growth retains intrinsic minima before
proportional expansion. This fixes merged-footer distortions reproduced by the
independent noWrap content controls.

## OpenType ligatures and legacy-only font kerning

ECMA-376 Part 1 §17.3.2.19 (`kern`) supplies the run's size threshold;
the existing `enableOpenTypeFeatures` compatibility switch gates effective
`w14:ligatures`. The native reference omits legacy kern-table pairs for enabled
OpenType ligatures in four independently tested legacy-only families when
explicit character spacing is zero. Expanded and condensed character spacing
retain the legacy kern pairs; two further 48-line native controls verify both
signs and keep tracked text unchanged. The
eight-font controls in `tests/fixtures/opentype-kerning` contrast both switch
values and none/standardContextual ligatures; the original four-font controls
also remain required. This is native compatibility evidence, not a claim that
the DOCX standard prescribes a font synthesis or shaping backend.

For an authorized local family whose selectable faces consistently have kern
without GPOS, preparation registers private in-memory faces without kern. The
browser still shapes the complete string, including fallback fonts with GPOS.
The initial Canvas fontKerning=none approach was rejected because it disabled
Cyrillic fallback kerning. Measurement and paint select the same derived face;
the separate synthetic-bold advance face receives the same table treatment.
Source declarations, font bytes and DOCX package parts are unchanged. Derived
font bytes are never stored, installed, exported or uploaded. Preparations are
cached and limited to enabled documents requesting ligatures and kerning.
Unknown, denied, variable or mixed-capability families retain prior behavior.

Weights, italic faces and the requested width subfamily are retained; condensed
siblings enumerated under the same local family cannot replace ordinary faces.
The derived SFNT rebuilds its directory/checksums and drops its stale signature.
Non-Macintosh cmap language metadata is normalized to zero, retaining glyph
mappings and Macintosh language fields, as required by the
[OpenType cmap specification](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/typography/opentype/spec/cmap#use-of-the-language-field-in-cmap-subtables).
This repairs legacy metadata that Windows accepts but browser font validation
rejects; independently authored SFNT tests cover the transformation.

The enabled eight-font control matches all 48 line origins within 0.2pt.
The disabled Palatino letter control separately exposes the native reference's legacy-versus-
GPOS selection difference and retains an expected-failure oracle. It is not
claimed fixed by omitting legacy-only kerning. Browser regressions also check
fallback pairs, styles, editable exports, untouched parts and exact undo.

The follow-up `legacy-kerning-pairs` fixture retains 112 native observations
with explicit no-ligature runs and both document OpenType modes. Four disabled
Palatino strings, including an internal-space pair, fail; the other 108 origins
pass. A diagnostic legacy-pair-to-GPOS conversion matches all 56 disabled widths
within 0.158pt, but is not shipped because it replaces unrelated positioning.
Selective kern lookup replacement, preserved mark/script features and a distinct
document-mode flag remain necessary before claiming this gap fixed. Native data,
strict expected failures and exact-package editing regressions are retained.

requests have a consistent solution.

preferences replace rather than repeat the prior proportional calculation.

### Text-bevel smoothing at shallow contour turns — 2026-09-26

Supported angle text bevels now interpolate illumination along a face when its
adjacent contour turn is below 30 degrees. Vertex normals are weighted by face
area (edge length for this fixed-width bevel); sharp corners retain separate
normals. Lighting is evaluated at the endpoints before interpolation and color
clipping. This affects the text 3D painter, not ordinary text or saved OOXML.

Ten independently drawn fork controls bracket 30 degrees and vary arm length.
Their temporary font uses original outlines and the already approved OFL-1.1
metadata headers; no font binary is shipped. Native reference exports and
50 stem samples are hash-bound in tests/fixtures/text-3d/bevel-smoothing-*.
The geometry/shader comparison matches every sample within one channel value.
MS-DOCX §§2.6.1.20/2.6.3.23 describe props3d, and ECMA-376 Part 1 §20.1.5.4
describes bevelT. These controls establish the native reference's interpolation behavior; no
normative synthetic-outline or smoothing algorithm is claimed or contradicted.

The initial per-pixel shading implementation added measurable uncached paint
cost and was revised before shipping. Even-odd scanline spans preserve concave
and crossing-face coverage while avoiding work outside the bevel; illumination
coefficients are prepared once per edge. Focused final timings show lower
subsequent uncached medians, but first-call results remain variable and are not
uniformly better. This is not a general no-regression performance guarantee.
Further timing work stays recorded rather than expanding this rendering fix.

Validation: 46 focused unit checks, 12 rendering/edit/export/undo browser
workflows, 159 schema checks across 25 packages, production build, and the
200-package license gate pass. The original ten native outline references are
unchanged after generalizing their fixture generator.

## Tab demand in AutoFit cell minima — September 27, 2026

ECMA-376 Part 1 §17.18.87 permits alternative AutoFit algorithms; indentation,
custom stops and default intervals are specified in §§17.3.1.12, 17.3.1.37–38
and 17.15.1.25. Original controls establish native intrinsic demand separately
from painted tab placement. Tabs contribute their advance and the first wrap
chunk of the following field. Legacy modes 12/14 use a zero measurement origin
and an implicit left-indent stop; mode 15 starts at the actual first-line
position. Leading legacy tabs can ignore a positive first-line indent. Decimal
stops are skipped for minimum demand, with default stops resuming beyond the
custom range. The generic writing reserve is not added again beyond nonempty
paragraph indentation. This is observed compatibility within AutoFit's
algorithm latitude, not a demonstrated normative contradiction.

ordinary and complex-script bold/italic declarations. The user command layer
now toggles both independently, based on the first selected character (or the
pending typing format at a caret), matching the native reference's commands. Direct
setRunFormat scalar edits remain independent; styles and serialization do not
silently synchronize dormant properties. Mixed selection commands now follow
the first character instead of treating mixed as uniformly off.

The original script-format-commands fixture covers 43 cases and 86 native
CommandBars.ExecuteMso observations, including opposite values and mixed runs.
All observations match in both forward and backward selections. Native ribbon
pressed states still read ordinary properties in these controls; there is no
evidence here for replacing the toolbar getter with a CS-only effective value.
The native source, saved outputs and results are hash-bound. This is a command
compatibility correction, not a claimed OOXML specification divergence.

Editable regressions cover pending typing, direct-property independence,
round trips, unrelated parts, exact undo, and toolbar/keyboard/beforeinput
entry points. No extra layout or shaping work is introduced. Full active
cs/rtl editing remains guarded; font-size commands and other script/font
editing cases still require native evidence.

choices are not emulated by this flag-only correction.

### Theme-color precision candidate rejected — September 27, 2026

A bounded comparison of hue/saturation/lightness quantization variants against
all three existing native sets found no exact candidate. Windows Shlwapi HLS
conversion with truncated transformed lightness matches only 108/512 shade
cases (rounded lightness: 58/512), so that platform API is not a substitute
for the native reference's arithmetic. Full-precision channel truncation and half-byte light
quantization also leave native mismatches.

The strongest tested hue/saturation variant rounds hue to 1/255, floors
saturation to 1/256, retains full lightness, and truncates final channels.
It matches 401/512 sweep, 102/128 precision and 104/128 boundary colors, leaving

it explicitly unsuitable for production. No color conversion was changed.

for an unresolved rendering defect, not a passing conformance test.

## SVG mask interpretation in the native reference (2026-09-27)

The native reference treats SVG masks as luminance masks even when mask-type is
explicitly alpha, in both presentation-attribute and inline CSS forms. This
is a divergence from CSS Masking 1 section 7.10.1 and section 9.2:
https://www.w3.org/TR/css-masking-1/#MaskValues
Alpha mode should use the alpha channel independently of mask color. The
preview clone now overrides computed alpha interpretation to luminance;
original SVG bytes and declarations remain unchanged in DOCX exports.

Two original fixtures, svg-mask-opacity and svg-mask-opacity-expanded, retain
12 reference-native metafile PNGs with source/native/image hashes. The three alpha
mode controls change from browser alpha 127/255/255 to native 0/0/128. Full,
cropped, grouped and shape-fill placements remain editable; exports preserve
media, relationships and other untouched parts, and undo restores exact parts.

These controls also narrow the unresolved edge behavior: opaque white/gray/blue
mask geometry has near-binary coverage (white alpha 0/254/255), while transparent
paint or groups retain graded coverage. Object/fill opacity .5 yields white
alpha 127, whereas group opacity .5 yields 128. Applying a blanket coverage

### SVG opaque-mask alpha omission — 2026-09-27 native evidence

CSS Masking Level 1 section 7.10.1 requires luminance multiplied by the
corresponding alpha and explicitly treats SVG graphics as RGBA:
https://www.w3.org/TR/css-masking-1/#MaskValues
the native reference diverges in the original opaque-fill controls: it takes
straight-RGB luminance without raster coverage alpha. Almost-opaque paint
and a translucent paint within the mask restore alpha weighting; zero-alpha
paint does not. The six svg-mask-opaque controls and identity-filter companions
reproduce this independently of a corpus document. The paired checker matches
every pixel across 18 cases, including the earlier opaque curved controls.

the native companion RGB already explains their mask pixels exactly. General
classification and browser rasterization remain unimplemented; gradients,
images and additional inherited paint combinations need verification. This is
a documented compatibility gap, not a completed feature or template #288 fix.

### SVG group byte composition (2026-09-27)

Within the existing SVG 1.1 section 14.5 translucent solid-group subset,
the renderer now follows native byte composition: truncate paint opacity,
apply coverage to premultiplied channels and alpha, composite with rounded
byte arithmetic, and store straight RGBA using a truncated 16-bit reciprocal.
Round group image opacity to a byte and apply each group's alpha separately.
Zero-opacity paints no longer expand the generated raster bounds. Original
SVG parts and authored opacity declarations remain intact in DOCX exports.

two-to-four-level opacity chains. Every decoded RGBA channel and raster bound
matches the native reference. They disprove the earlier opacity-folding and universal
ties-to-even candidates. Six existing rectangle-edge controls still match,
and the corrected diagnostic also retains exact alpha across 84 mask controls.
Curve geometry, unsupported paints and resource limits retain their existing
paths; this does not implement general mask rasterization or image resampling.

## Overflowing legacy kerning tables — 2026-09-29

ECMA-376 Part 1 §§17.3.2.19 (`kern`) and 17.3.2.26 (`rFonts`) govern
the run's kerning request and family. Font-format recovery follows the OpenType
`kern` specification: format-0 records are sorted pairs, subtable lengths are
unsigned 16-bit values, and horizontal subtables may add their adjustments.
The native reference accepts a legacy font whose single subtable length wraps that limit;
the browser drops its pairs. This is font compatibility, not a new OOXML rule.

The already-authorized legacy-font path now creates a private conforming copy
only when the sorted pair count, exact table size, horizontal coverage and
wrapped length prove that particular overflow. It splits every original pair
into valid-length subtables and removes a proven empty GPOS. Variable, active
GPOS, ambiguous and mixed recoverable/unrecoverable families retain fallback.
No font enumeration, remote source or shipped font binary is added. Original
font and DOCX bytes are preserved; kerning-disabled/OpenType selection is unchanged.

The manually authored reviewed-family DOCX and native reference EMF display oracle show
maximum matching-font error reduced from 1.22pt to 0.281pt. All four styled
paragraphs improve; continuation lines without affected pairs are unchanged.
The strict 0.25pt display and existing 0.35pt PDF oracles remain expected
failures. This is not full glyph fidelity or a bundled Open Sans replacement.
See `tests/fixtures/empty-gpos-kerning/README.md` for provenance, independent
reference recording, supported subset, and remaining OpenType-mode limits.

Local unit, browser editing/round-trip, XSD and build checks accompany this

### Face-dependent script sizing (2026-09-29)

ECMA-376 Part 1 §17.3.2.42 (`vertAlign`) requires reduced/repositioned text
without changing the stored point size; it does not prescribe the numerical
scaling rule. The native reference controls in `tests/fixtures/script-size` and
`tests/fixtures/script-metric-controls` establish a face-dependent sizing rule
for the 144 recorded static-font cases. This is implementation behavior, not
a demonstrated contradiction of OOXML.

The renderer reads recommended vertical script size and superscript offset
from OS/2 metadata. The native reference's observed fallback is selected when the superscript
offset satisfies `round(2 * size * offset / unitsPerEm) < floor(size / 2)`;
that branch uses 60% for both script directions. Otherwise the respective
vertical size recommendation applies. The reduced size is rounded to half
points and used uniformly in both axes. Original size, XML and script position
are retained. The 0.061 pt native PDF comparison tolerance accounts for the
recorded PDF text-matrix quantization; it is not a layout-error allowance.

Only fonts already authorized by the browser, or existing same-origin font
sources, are read. No automatic permission prompt or font-byte persistence is
introduced. Missing/invalid/variable metrics retain the previous fallback.
Font-family resolution precedes metadata reads; those reads overlap existing
font preparation. Authoring script after opening queues the existing relayout
callback without changing history. Small caps, absolute character spacing,
text-width scaling and enlarged outline measurement retain the authored
reference size rather than reapplying half-point rounding at measurement size.

Script baseline and italic-origin behavior remain open; this change addresses
size and advance only.


### Pointer selection into restored inline prompts (2026-09-29)

ECMA-376 Part 1 17.5.2.26/31 and 17.5.2.25/39 define inline SDT/content and
placeholder markup without prescribing mouse selection transitions. Eight
independent saved reference controls establish that an ordinary exit click landing
inside the restored prompt selects through the originally targeted word's end,
mapped through the inserted text. It does not select the whole original line
or paragraph. Manual-break and automatic-wrap holdouts distinguish these rules.

The pointer handler retains that original word boundary before restoration and
uses it only when the new hit belongs to the same restored control. Stored
content and package parts are unchanged. Later clicks, modifiers, read-only
guards and drag behavior keep their existing paths. This is native editing
compatibility, not a claimed conflict with a normative OOXML mouse rule.

Local validation covers 36 distinct browser scenarios, 99 unit checks (three
initial timeouts passed in an isolated retry without changing limits), 254 XML
checks, build and licensing. The original #137 remains pixel-identical and
passes edit/export/undo/reopen. Bounded paired timings show no consistent slowdown. Shift-click,
same-offset edge exits and broader drag selection still require native work.

ECMA-376 Part 1 §§17.5.2.26/31 and 17.5.2.25/39 define the SDT/content and

### Empty-control pointer ownership at story end (2026-09-29)

Ordinary clicks and completed drags beyond the final text now retain an outside caret after a terminal empty inline content control. Leaving its inside caret restores the prompt even at the same logical offset; subsequent typing stays outside the restored prompt. Internal paragraph ends retain their existing inside behavior. ECMA-376 Part 1 §§17.5.2.26/31 (`sdt`/`sdtContent`) and §§17.5.2.25/39 (`placeholder`/`showingPlcHdr`) define the preserved markup; pointer policy is observed reference compatibility, not a normative OOXML algorithm. Ten independent native reference results, browser editing/round-trip guards, and schema validation cover this behavior. Modified interactions retain their existing behavior. This does not complete all control interaction support.

### Extended selections from empty inline controls (2026-09-29)

Shift+Left/Right now retain the first zero-length control boundary before selecting neighboring text. Continuing in the same direction restores the prompt and maps the focus through the insertion while keeping the original anchor. Typing retains the native control ownership; backward replacement leaves the restored spaces and commits their placeholder state. Selection metadata is separate from DOCX, survives normalization around unrelated atomic fields, and participates in undo. Seven hash-bound reference controls cover both directions, consecutive extension, undo continuation, and the intermediate restored placeholder. ECMA-376 Part 1 §§17.5.2.26/31 and §§17.5.2.25/39 define the retained markup, not a normative keyboard algorithm. General Shift-click and broader nonempty/adjacent-control selection remain open.

### Local image decoding recovery (2026-09-29)

Document opening now isolates raster and drawing-preview decode failures. It retains successfully decoded assets and the imported document structure, reports the failed asset ID, and opens read-only. Unavailable body images keep their authored layout space; they currently have no painted placeholder. A failed picture background retains the solid page color. Original download remains byte-for-byte intact. Strict decoding remains the default for editing operations, and aggregate resource limits remain enforced. Font refresh in read-only previews retains independent healthy assets and reports failed ones.

The independently authored [image recovery controls](../tests/fixtures/image-recovery/README.md) contain a styled heading, two pictures, table, numbering, a header, and nondefault page geometry. XML import, layout validation, malformed image metadata, and aggregate resource-limit failures can still reach the document-wide fallback. This does not complete the broader recovery backlog.

Unsupported block content, some style/placement interactions and structural failures can still fall back at a wider boundary.
